analysis.one_liner: Restores federally funded health benefits to retired coal miners who lost them in 2018 bankruptcies.
analysis.headline: The bill advanced through committee without recorded opposition — ordered reported by voice vote on October 23, 2019 — but never reached the House floor and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: When union coal companies went through bankruptcy in 2018, some retired miners' health benefits were denied or cut. Current law already directs the Treasury to transfer money into the miners' Multiemployer Health Benefit Plan to cover retirees who lost benefits in the 2012 and 2015 bankruptcies. This bill would add the 2018 bankruptcy victims to that group and pay for them the same way, so their health coverage would be made whole from federal funds rather than from the bankrupt companies.
analysis.who_benefits: Retired union coal miners and their surviving spouses whose health benefits were denied or reduced when their employers went through bankruptcy in 2018. Instead of losing coverage mid-retirement because a company restructured, they would be covered by the same federal transfer that already protects miners affected by the 2012 and 2015 bankruptcies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retired union coal miners hit by 2018 bankruptcies

how_it_helps.text: Adds miners affected by coal company bankruptcies begun in 2018 to the group whose lost benefits are counted when Treasury calculates its transfer to the Multiemployer Health Benefit Plan, alongside those affected by the 2012 and 2015 bankruptcies.

Covers workers under any UMWA wage agreement whose employer was a signatory or a debtor consolidated with a signatory's bankruptcy — not just the narrowly defined group in the 2017 version of the law.
Applies to fiscal years beginning after September 30, 2018, so it reaches back to the 2018 bankruptcies themselves rather than starting fresh.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through a larger Treasury transfer into the miners' retiree health plan. The bill does not send the bill to the coal companies that exited bankruptcy having shed these obligations; the government picks up the cost of coverage the companies no longer fund.

drawbacks.text: The benefits are paid with additional federal transfers from the Treasury, so adding 2018-bankruptcy miners increases federal spending on retiree health care rather than recouping it from the companies involved.

The bill backfills benefits after companies shed them in bankruptcy; it does not change the bankruptcy or funding rules that allowed the obligations to be abandoned in the first place, so the same gap could open again in the next industry restructuring.

Coverage is limited to miners covered by United Mine Workers wage agreements with signatory operators or debtors consolidated with a signatory's bankruptcy; retired miners whose employers were not union signatories get nothing from this bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is a federal outlay to keep health coverage promised to miners whose employers walked away from it in bankruptcy — a population with no replacement employer and often no other coverage. The bill is narrow and does not fix the underlying bankruptcy mechanics, and it leaves non-union retirees out, but on its own terms it makes a targeted, honest repair to a broken promise at federal expense rather than company expense.

outcome.mechanism: The House Natural Resources Committee ordered the bill reported by voice vote in October 2019, but the House never took it up, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 31, 2019 by Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia and referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
It drew 40 cosponsors, 35 House Democrats and 5 House Republicans.

The Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources held a hearing on July 24, 2019, and on October 23, 2019 the subcommittee was discharged and the full committee held a markup, ordering the bill to be reported by voice vote.
No further action followed: the bill was never reported to the House floor, never received a vote, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal companies whose 2018 bankruptcies shifted retiree health costs onto the government are better off than if the bill had passed, since the bill would have formalized federal responsibility for those benefits without charging the industry. Retired miners affected by the 2018 bankruptcies were left to wait for Congress to address their coverage through other legislation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal operators that shed retiree health obligations

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 40 cosponsors split 35 Democrats and 5 Republicans, and the committee advanced it by voice vote; the record shows no vote and no recorded opponent, only that the bill never received House floor time.

industries.industry: UMWA retiree health fund (Multiemployer Health Benefit Plan)
industries.note: The bill expands the plan's covered population — miners hit by 2018 bankruptcies — and enlarges the federal transfer that funds it. For the retirees it covers, that means health benefits made whole at government expense.

The bill does not restore the retirees to the companies' books, so operators pay nothing; a federal backstop for miners who lost benefits in bankruptcy also removes some pressure to secure company funding for legacy obligations. Miners get coverage; taxpayers absorb the cost the companies shed.
